fd <- trend[trend$indicator == "rh_del_facility", ]
cs_at <- function(s) cs$estimate[cs$survey_id == s]
fd_at <- function(s) fd$estimate[fd$survey_id == s]
iq <- function(s, m, col = "estimate") ineq[ineq$survey_id == s & ineq$measure == m, col]
dc <- function(from, by, comp, col = "estimate") dec[dec$from == from & dec$by == by & dec$component == comp, col]
ch <- function(i, a, b, col) chg[chg$indicator == i & chg$survey_1 == a & chg$survey_2 == b, col]
p <- function(name, survey, col = "naive", group = NULL) {
  r <- pit[pit$pitfall == name & pit$survey_id == survey, ]
  if (!is.null(group)) r <- r[r$group == group, ]
  r[[col]][1]
}
qv <- function(s, col) qual[[col]][qual$survey_id == s]
n_margins <- sum(syn$margins)
yr4 <- function(x) sub("^BD(\\d{4})DHS$", "\\1", x)

# Abstract

```{asis, echo = cureus}
**Introduction:** Secondary analyses of the Bangladesh Demographic and Health
Survey (BDHS) are common, but their estimates are rarely checked against the
official values, and several features of the survey are easy to mishandle.
We assessed how closely official BDHS estimates can be reproduced, how much
common analytic errors matter, and how data quality has changed since 1993.

**Methods:** We developed bdhs, an open-source R package covering all nine
BDHS rounds (1993-94 to 2022), and used it to recompute every indicator with
a published national value from the original recode files. We quantified
common analytic errors, design effects and data quality, developed synthetic
data calibrated to the official estimates, and analysed the rise of
caesarean delivery from 2004 to 2022.

**Results:** Of 355 national estimates, 353 matched the official value
(median absolute difference 0.03 percentage points). Ignoring the 2022 short
questionnaire lowered unmet need for family planning from 10.0% to 6.7%, and
treating the ever-married sample as all women inflated child marriage by
about ten percentage points. Ignoring the sample design made standard errors
up to 1.8 times too small. Caesarean delivery rose from 4.5% to 44.0%, about
80% of it within education groups. Synthetic data reproduced 1,278 official
values within 0.21 percentage points.

**Conclusions:** Official BDHS estimates can be reproduced almost exactly
when the ever-married sample, questionnaire changes and survey design are
handled correctly. The bdhs package makes these decisions explicit and
checkable.
```

```{asis, echo = sji}
Secondary analyses of Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) microdata are rarely
checked against the official estimates they should reproduce. We developed
bdhs, an open-source R package covering all nine rounds of the Bangladesh
Demographic and Health Survey (1993-94 to 2022), and used it to assess how
closely official statistics can be reproduced from the released recode files.
Of 355 national estimates recomputed across eight rounds, 353 matched the
published value, with a median absolute difference of 0.03 percentage points.
The validation exposed analytic pitfalls that change results substantially:
ignoring the 2022 short questionnaire understated unmet need for family
planning by a third, and treating the ever-married sample as all women
overstated child marriage by about ten percentage points. Ignoring the sample
design made standard errors up to 1.8 times too small. We also present a
method for generating synthetic microdata from published aggregates only,
which reproduced 1,278 official estimates within 0.21 percentage points and
contains no respondent information. Making these decisions explicit in
validated software allows official statistics to be reproduced, checked and
taught without access to restricted data.
```

```{asis, echo = !cureus && !sji}
**Background:** The Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) has been
conducted nine times since 1993 and is the main source of population and
health statistics for the country. Secondary analyses of the respondent-level
files are common, but their estimates are rarely checked against the
officially published values, and several features of the survey design are
easy to mishandle. We assessed how closely the official estimates can be
reproduced from the recode files, how much common analytic errors change the
results, how data quality has changed across rounds, and whether synthetic
data calibrated to the published estimates can reproduce them.

**Methods:** We built bdhs, an open-source R package covering every BDHS
round from 1993-94 to 2022. It bundles all official estimates published
through the DHS Program and provides tools for the licensed microdata: file
identification, cross-round harmonisation, complex survey designs, 97
indicator definitions, fertility and mortality rates, data-quality
diagnostics, and inequality, trend and decomposition analysis. Using the
original recode files, we recomputed every indicator with a published
national value and counted an estimate as matching if it was within 0.5
percentage points of the official value, allowing for rounding. We then
quantified the effect of common analytic errors, estimated design effects and
assessed data quality across rounds. We also developed a method for
generating synthetic BDHS data calibrated to the official estimates and
illustrated the analytic tools with the rise of caesarean delivery between
2004 and 2022.

**Results:** Of 355 national estimates computed across eight rounds, 353
matched the official value (median absolute difference 0.03 percentage
points). Counting women who received the short 2022 questionnaire as having
no unmet need for family planning lowered the estimate from 10.0% to 6.7%,
and treating the ever-married sample as all women inflated child marriage by
about ten percentage points. Design effects of 1.6 to 3.1 meant that ignoring
the sample design made standard errors up to 1.8 times too small. Data
quality improved over time, although height-for-age z-scores remained more
dispersed than expected and ages at death were heaped at 12 months. Caesarean
delivery rose from 4.5% in 2004 to 44.0% in 2022; about 80% of this increase
occurred within education groups rather than through changes in mothers'
education. Synthetic data reproduced 1,278 official national and subnational
values with a maximum deviation of 0.21 percentage points.

**Conclusions:** Official BDHS estimates can be reproduced almost exactly
from the recode files, but only when the ever-married sample, questionnaire
changes such as the 2022 short questionnaire, and the survey design are
handled correctly. The bdhs package makes these decisions explicit and
checkable. Calibrated synthetic data allows methods to be taught and analysis
code to be shared without the restricted files, although they do not
preserve associations between variables.
```

**Keywords:** Demographic and Health Surveys; Bangladesh; complex survey
design; reproducibility; validation; synthetic data; health inequality; R

# `r if (cureus || sji) "Introduction" else "Background"`

Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) provide much of what is known about
fertility, family planning, maternal and child health and nutrition in low-
and middle-income countries. Bangladesh has taken part since the early 1990s
and has now completed nine rounds: 1993-94, 1996-97, 1999-2000, 2004, 2007,
2011, 2014, 2017-18 and 2022. The surveys are carried out by the National
Institute of Population Research and Training (NIPORT) with technical
assistance from ICF [@niport2024]. Official estimates appear in the final
reports and through the DHS Program's online tools, while the
respondent-level files are released to registered researchers.

These files support a large secondary literature, yet published estimates
from them are seldom compared with the official figures. When they differ,
readers cannot tell whether the difference is substantive or simply a
computational slip. The definitions in the Guide to DHS Statistics
[@croft2018] are clear, but applying them to Bangladesh requires attention to
details that are not visible in the data files. The women's samples are
restricted to women who have ever been married, so indicators for all women
need adjustment factors. Division boundaries and codes changed three times
between rounds. The 2022 survey gave a third of women a shortened
questionnaire. Some questions are specific to Bangladesh and do not belong in
the standard definitions. An error at any of these points carries through to
the published result without warning.

Several tools already help with parts of this work. The rdhs package gives
access to the DHS Program's data and indicator services [@watson2019],
DHS.rates computes fertility and childhood mortality rates [@dhsrates], the
survey package implements design-based estimation [@lumley2004], and
IPUMS-DHS distributes harmonised extracts of selected variables across
countries [@ipumsdhs]. What is missing is a way to check an analysis of the
original files against the official estimates, a record of the
country-specific decisions this requires, and a way to share reproducible
analyses when the data themselves cannot be shared.

This paper introduces bdhs, a package for R [@rcore] that covers all BDHS
rounds and uses it to answer four questions. How closely can the official
estimates be reproduced from the recode files? How much do common analytic
errors change the results? What does a systematic data-quality assessment
show across rounds? And can synthetic data reproduce the published estimates
closely enough to be useful for teaching and for testing analysis code? We
illustrate the trend, inequality and decomposition tools with the rise of
caesarean delivery between 2004 and 2022, and the bundled official estimates
with an assessment of progress towards selected Sustainable Development Goal
(SDG) targets.

# `r if (cureus) "Materials & Methods" else "Methods"`

## Data

The package bundles all 310,528 official estimates published for Bangladesh
through the DHS Program's indicator service, covering every indicator, round
and breakdown. It also bundles the definitions of 2,607 indicators,
catalogues of the 13 Bangladesh surveys listed by the DHS Program (the nine
BDHS rounds and other surveys) and their 441 data files, codebooks with
variable names and labels but no respondent values, and the division
boundaries used in each survey. No respondent-level data is distributed, in
line with the DHS terms of use.

The analyses in this paper used our licensed copies of the recode files: the
children's recode for 1993-94, 1999-2000, 2004, 2007, 2011, 2014, 2017-18 and
2022; the births, household, women's and household-member recode for 2017-18;
and the women's and household-member recodes for 2022. No recode files from
1996-97 were analysed, so that round is not included in the validation, and
for rounds before 2017-18 only indicators from the children recode could be
checked. Only aggregate results are reported, and the analysis scripts are
publicly available.

## The bdhs package

bdhs identifies DHS files by their names or, for renamed files, by their
contents, and keeps a fast local copy. It harmonises 112 variables across
rounds using 1,008 round-specific rules. Each rule is checked against the
value labels in the data, so a recoding error raises a warning instead of
passing silently. Survey designs use the DHS sampling-error strata, the
enumeration areas as primary sampling units, and normalised sample weights.
Pooled analyses keep each round's strata and clusters separate and offer
normalised, de-normalised and equal weighting.

Indicators are defined in code. Each definition records the denominator,
reference period, recode file, weight and, where needed, the all-woman
factor. A single function call therefore returns any of the 97 indicators
with design-based standard errors. Fertility and childhood mortality rates
use the DHS synthetic-cohort methods with jackknife standard errors. The
package documentation lists every function.

## Validation

For every indicator with an official value, we computed the national
estimate from each available recode file and compared it with the official
value for the same reference period. A comparison passed if the absolute
difference was no more than 0.5 percentage points (or the equivalent for
rates), plus half a unit of the precision to which the official value is
rounded. For a value published to one decimal place, for example, the
tolerance is 0.55 points, which is why a matched estimate can differ by
slightly more than 0.5 points (Table 1). This tolerance is smaller than the
design-based standard error of most headline indicators (Table 3), so any
accepted difference is small relative to the survey's own uncertainty.

## Analytic pitfalls and design effects

Whenever an analytic decision changed a result during validation, we kept
both versions: the estimate a straightforward but naive analysis gives, and
the correct one that reproduces the official value. A naive analysis here
means one that overlooks a feature of the Bangladesh data, such as the
ever-married sample, a questionnaire change or the sampling weights. The
pitfalls in Table 2 are therefore the decisions we encountered while
reproducing the official estimates, not a systematic review of errors in the
published literature. Design effects for headline indicators were computed
as the ratio of the design-based variance to the variance under simple
random sampling with the same number of observations; the square root of the
design effect is the factor by which a simple-random-sample analysis
understates the standard error.

## Data quality

The data-quality module implements the standard DHS diagnostics
[@pullum2006]. These cover:

- age heaping in the household roster, measured by the Whipple index for
  ages 23-62 and by Myers' blended index;
- the ratio of women recorded at age 50 to those at 49, which detects ages
  being shifted at the upper boundary of eligibility for the women's
  interview;
- completeness of birth dates;
- the ratio of births in the fifth year before the survey to those in the
  fourth year, which detects births being displaced out of the window for
  the health questions;
- heaping of reported ages at death at 12 months;
- the dispersion of anthropometric z-scores, the share of flagged values and
  terminal-digit preference in measured height [@who2019anthro].

As in the DHS data-quality tables, these statistics are unweighted.

## Calibrated synthetic data

Synthetic data is generated without access to any microdata, in three steps.

1. **Structure.** A synthetic population is created with the same files,
   variables, codes, labels, clusters, strata and weights as the real survey.
   Its size and its allocation to division-by-residence strata follow the
   official sample sizes and weighted distributions.
2. **Calibration.** For each target indicator (four to seven per recode file,
   for example facility delivery, contraceptive use and child stunting), the
   probability of the outcome in each division-by-residence cell is modelled
   on the logit scale as an intercept plus a division effect and a residence
   effect. These effects are found by iterative proportional fitting
   [@deming1940], so that the weighted national, division and residence
   values equal the official estimates for the indicator's reference period.
3. **Assignment.** Outcomes are assigned deterministically within cells, so
   the calibrated values are reproduced up to rounding rather than up to
   random error. Stratum weights are then raked to the official denominators
   of all targets.

The idea follows fully synthetic data for statistical disclosure limitation
[@rubin1993; @raghunathan2003], with one important difference: it uses only
published aggregates, so the synthetic files contain no information about
any respondent. They reproduce the calibrated values, but not the
associations between indicators or the variables that were not calibrated.

The synthetic files are therefore suited to teaching, to developing and
testing analysis code, and to sharing reproducible workflows, but not to
estimating relationships between variables or evaluating statistical models.

## Trends, inequality and decomposition

Changes between rounds were tested as differences between independent survey
estimates and expressed per year using the midpoints of fieldwork. Within a
round, contrasts between groups used the full design-based covariance matrix.

Inequality by household wealth was measured with:

- the difference and the ratio between the richest and poorest quintiles;
- the slope and relative indices of inequality, estimated by design-based
  regression on the weighted ridit of the wealth quintiles [@barros2013];
- the concentration index [@wagstaff1991; @kakwani1997], and for binary
  outcomes Erreygers' corrected index [@erreygers2009].

Changes between two rounds were split into a part due to shifts in the
composition of mothers and a part due to changes within groups, using
Kitagawa's method with symmetric weights [@kitagawa1955; @dasgupta1993] and
delete-one-cluster jackknife standard errors.

Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) was assessed from
the official estimates by comparing the average annual rate of change since
2014 with the rate needed to reach each 2030 target. Where no numerical SDG
target exists, published benchmarks were used [@fabic2015].

Because these calculations use only the official estimates bundled with the
package, they can be reproduced without access to any microdata.

All analyses were done in R [@rcore] with bdhs version 0.2.0 and the survey
package [@lumley2004].

# Results

## Agreement with the official estimates

Of the 355 national estimates we could compute, 353 matched the official
value (Table 1). The median absolute difference was 0.03 percentage points,
and it was below 0.04 points in every round. The two estimates that did not
match were women's thinness and overweight in 2022 computed from the women's
recode. The DHS Program calculates these from the household-member recode,
which includes all women in the biomarker subsample rather than only those
who have ever been married. Computed from that file, both match the official
values.

```{r tab1}
t1 <- vbr
t1$survey_id <- yr4(t1$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t1, col.names = c("Survey", "Recode files", "Estimates", "Matched",
                               "Median absolute difference", "Largest difference among matches"),
             caption = "Table 1. Agreement between estimates computed with bdhs and the official DHS values (percentage points)")
```

## How much common errors matter

Table 2 shows, for each pitfall we identified, the estimate from a naive
analysis next to the correct estimate. The two largest errors come from the
structure of the sample.

Every BDHS women's sample consists of women who have ever been married.
Analysing it as if it represented all women puts the share of women aged
20-24 who married before 18 at 68.8% in 2017-18; the correct figure is
58.9%.

In 2022, a third of women answered a short questionnaire with no family
planning questions. Counting them as having no unmet need gives 6.7% instead
of 10.0%.

The other pitfalls produced smaller but still material differences:

- counting the country-specific liquids lowers exclusive breastfeeding in
  2007 from 49.8% to 42.9%;
- leaving out births to mothers under 15 lowers the general fertility rate;
- ignoring the measles-rubella vaccine lowers measles coverage;
- using the subgroup all-woman factor for child marriage, rather than the
  total factor that the official tables use for every subgroup, shifts the
  urban estimate by 2.5 points.

Division codes add a trap of a different kind: code 5 means Rajshahi in 2014
but Mymensingh in 2017-18, so comparing codes across rounds compares
different places.

```{r tab2}
t2 <- pit[!is.na(pit$naive), c("pitfall", "survey_id", "group", "naive", "correct", "official")]
t2$survey_id <- yr4(t2$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t2, row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Pitfall", "Survey", "Group", "Naive estimate", "Correct estimate", "Official value"),
             caption = "Table 2. Effect of common analytic errors on BDHS estimates. Values are percentages, except the general fertility rate, which is births per 1,000 women.")
```

Design effects for headline indicators ranged from 1.6 to 3.1 (Table 3). An
analysis that treats the survey as a simple random sample would therefore
report confidence intervals up to 1.8 times too narrow. The largest design
effects were for delivery care, which is strongly clustered by area.

```{r tab3}
t3 <- deff
t3$survey_id <- yr4(t3$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Survey", "Indicator", "Estimate (%)", "SE, design-based", "SE, simple random sample", "Design effect", "n"),
             caption = "Table 3. Design effects for headline indicators. rh_del_csection, caesarean delivery; rh_del_facility, delivery in a health facility; rh_anc_4plus, four or more antenatal care visits; nt_stunting, stunting in children under 5; fp_cpr_modern, modern contraceptive use; ch_vac_basic, basic vaccination coverage. SE, standard error (percentage points).")
```

## Data quality

Birth dates were reported almost completely in every round, and we found no
sign of births being shifted out of the five-year window for the health
questions (Table 4). Anthropometric quality improved considerably. Flagged
height-for-age z-scores fell from 7.7% in 2007 to 0.3% in 2022. Child heights
ending in 0 or 5 fell from 31.6% in 1999-2000 to 17.4% in 2022, close to the
20% expected without digit preference. Even so, the standard deviation of
height-for-age z-scores stayed between 1.27 and 1.41, above the range of 1.0
to 1.2 expected for good-quality data [@who2019anthro].

Age reporting in the household roster was much less precise for men than for
women. In 2017-18 the Whipple index was 264 for men and 114 for women, where
100 means no heaping and 500 means every age ends in 0 or 5. By 2022 heaping
had fallen for men (216) but risen for women (137). Far fewer women were
recorded at age 50 than at 49, with ratios of 0.31 in 2017-18 and 0.61 in
2022 against about 1 expected, which suggests that some women's ages were
moved above the upper limit of eligibility for the women's interview. Ages at
death were heaped at 12 months, with a heaping index of 228 in 2017-18 and
179 in 2022 (100 means no heaping); this heaping can shift deaths between the
infant and child age groups.

```{r tab4}
t4 <- qual
t4$survey_id <- yr4(t4$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t4, row.names = FALSE, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Survey", "Birth dates complete (%)", "SD of height-for-age z", "Flagged height-for-age (%)",
                           "Heights ending in 0 or 5 (%)", "Whipple index, men", "Whipple index, women",
                           "Women aged 50 : 49", "Heaping of deaths at 12 months"),
             caption = "Table 4. Data-quality indicators by survey round (unweighted). A dash means the statistic needs a recode file that was not available.")
```

## Calibrated synthetic data

Synthetic files were generated for every round and for the children's,
women's and household-member recodes. Together they reproduced 1,278
official national, division and residence values. Because the outcomes are
calibrated to these values, close agreement is expected by design; the check
confirms that the calibration and the raking of the weights converged for
every file. The mean absolute deviation per round and file ranged from 0.01
to 0.07 percentage points, and the largest single deviation was 0.21 points
(Table 5, Figure 1). A full-size file took between 2.1 and 7.8 seconds to
generate.

```{r tab5}
t5 <- syn
t5$survey_id <- yr4(t5$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t5, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Survey", "Recode", "Indicators calibrated", "Values reproduced", "Records",
                           "Mean absolute deviation", "Largest deviation", "Seconds"),
             caption = "Table 5. Agreement of calibrated synthetic data with the official estimates (percentage points)")
```

```{r fig1, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = if (!sub) "Figure 1. Official estimates and the corresponding estimates from calibrated synthetic data, for every calibrated indicator, survey round and margin (national, division and residence). The line marks perfect agreement."}
g1 <- ggplot(syn_d, aes(official, synthetic)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Official estimate (%)", y = "Synthetic-data estimate (%)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
save_fig(g1, "Figure1", 5.5, 5.2)
```

## Case study: caesarean delivery, 2004-2022

`r if (sji) "Rony et al. examined" else "We previously examined"` the determinants of caesarean section in Bangladesh
over the same period with survey-weighted logistic regression [@rony2026].
Here the same trend is used to illustrate the package's descriptive tools:
change between rounds, wealth-related inequality and decomposition.

The share of births delivered by caesarean section rose from 4.5% in 2004 to
44.0% in 2022 (Figure 2), an increase of 39.5 percentage points, or 2.13
points a year. Every change between consecutive rounds was statistically
significant. Relative to its starting level, facility delivery grew more
slowly than caesarean delivery, so that by 2022 about 69% of births in health
facilities were by caesarean section (44.0% of all births against 63.5%
delivered in a facility).

```{r fig2, fig.width = 6.2, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = if (!sub) "Figure 2. Caesarean and facility delivery among births in the three years before each survey, Bangladesh 1999-2000 to 2022. Vertical bars show 95% confidence intervals."}
yr <- c(BD2000DHS = 2000, BD2004DHS = 2004, BD2007DHS = 2007, BD2011DHS = 2011,
        BD2014DHS = 2014, BD2017DHS = 2018, BD2022DHS = 2022)
d <- trend
d$year <- yr[d$survey_id]
d$what <- ifelse(d$indicator == "rh_del_csection", "Caesarean delivery", "Facility delivery")
g2 <- ggplot(d, aes(year, estimate, colour = what)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Percentage of births", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
save_fig(g2, "Figure2", 6.2, 3.4)
```

Absolute inequality by wealth grew as caesarean delivery spread. The slope
index of inequality rose from 18.3 percentage points in 2004 to 56.0 in
2017-18 and stood at 53.1 (95% CI 47.5 to 58.7) in 2022. Relative inequality
moved the other way. The relative index of inequality fell from 469.6 in
2004, when caesarean delivery was rare in the poorest households, to 3.4 in
2022, as women in the poorest households increasingly delivered by caesarean
section (Table 6). Every index computed from the microdata agreed closely
with the same index derived from the official estimates by wealth quintile;
in 2022, for example, Erreygers' index was 0.339 by both methods.

```{r tab6}
t6 <- ineq[ineq$measure %in% c("difference", "sii", "rii", "eci"), c("survey_id", "measure", "estimate")]
t6 <- reshape(t6, idvar = "survey_id", timevar = "measure", direction = "wide")
names(t6) <- sub("estimate.", "", names(t6), fixed = TRUE)
t6$survey_id <- yr4(t6$survey_id)
t6 <- t6[, c("survey_id", "difference", "sii", "rii", "eci")]
knitr::kable(t6, row.names = FALSE, digits = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 3),
             col.names = c("Survey", "Richest minus poorest (points)", "Slope index of inequality",
                           "Relative index of inequality", "Erreygers concentration index"),
             caption = "Table 6. Wealth-related inequality in caesarean delivery")
```

Changes in the characteristics of mothers explained only a small part of the
increase (Table 7). Between 2004 and 2022, the shift towards more educated
mothers accounted for 7.7 of the 39.5 percentage-point increase (20%), and
changes in the wealth distribution of 0.8 points (2%). The remaining 80% to
98% reflected higher caesarean rates within education and wealth groups. The
pattern was similar between 2017-18 and 2022, when composition accounted for
10% of the 11.3-point increase by education and none of it by wealth
(-3.5%). These components describe how the change is distributed and should
not be read as causal effects.

```{r tab7}
t7 <- dec
t7$period <- paste(sub("BD(\\d{4}).*", "\\1", t7$from), sub("BD(\\d{4}).*", "\\1", t7$to), sep = " to ")
t7$by <- ifelse(t7$by == "mother_edu_level", "Mother's education", "Wealth quintile")
t7$component <- c(composition = "Composition", within = "Within groups", total = "Total change")[t7$component]
knitr::kable(t7[, c("period", "by", "component", "estimate", "se", "percent")], row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Period", "Decomposed by", "Component", "Percentage points", "SE", "Share of change (%)"),
             caption = "Table 7. Decomposition of the change in caesarean delivery")
```

## Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals

On the official estimates, under-five mortality and child stunting were on
course to meet their 2030 targets (Table 8). Neonatal mortality, wasting and
skilled attendance at birth were not. Child marriage was falling but remained
far from elimination.

```{r tab8}
t8 <- sdg[, c("sdg", "name", "baseline_value", "latest_value", "target", "aarc", "required_aarc", "on_track")]
t8$on_track <- ifelse(is.na(t8$on_track), "–", ifelse(t8$on_track, "Yes", "No"))
knitr::kable(t8, row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("SDG", "Indicator", "2014", "2022", "Target", "Annual change (%)",
                           "Required annual change (%)", "On track"),
             caption = "Table 8. Progress towards SDG-related targets, from the official estimates")
```

# Discussion

This study shows that the official BDHS estimates can be reproduced from the
recode files almost exactly, as long as a handful of decisions are made
correctly. Once the survey design, denominators, reference periods and
round-specific rules were written down in code, 353 of 355 national estimates
matched the published values, most of them to within a few hundredths of a
percentage point. Inequality measures computed from the microdata also
agreed with those derived from the official tables. The same exercise showed
that the decisions that matter most are ones the data files do not reveal.

The largest errors come from how the sample was drawn, not from the
statistical method. Because every BDHS women's sample is limited to women who
have ever been married, child marriage estimated without all-woman factors
comes out about ten percentage points too high. Bangladesh's child-marriage
problem is serious enough without overstating it. In 2022 the error runs the
other way: counting women who were never asked about family planning as
having no unmet need understates it by a third and would suggest much faster
progress since 2017-18 than actually took place.

Other conventions matter less but are still worth getting right. Some are
documented only implicitly, in the way the official tables were produced. The
child-marriage tables use the total all-woman factor for every subgroup,
while the subgroup factors are used elsewhere. The exclusive breastfeeding
indicator leaves out the country-specific liquids that the questionnaire
records. Neither choice can be inferred from the data documentation alone,
and each moves estimates by more than their sampling error.

Design effects of 1.6 to 3.1 are typical of DHS surveys but are still often
ignored. Treating the BDHS as a simple random sample makes estimates look
more precise than they are, which matters most when comparing subgroups or
rounds. Regional comparisons over time raise a further, practical problem:
because divisions were renumbered when Mymensingh division was created, the
same code refers to different places in different rounds. Any regional trend
analysis needs harmonised division boundaries.

The data-quality assessment is mostly reassuring. Birth histories are
complete, and there is no sign of the displacement of births out of the
health-question window that distorts estimates in some DHS countries.
Anthropometric measurement improved markedly after 2011, which supports the
comparability of recent nutrition estimates. Three patterns deserve
attention, and all are consistent with earlier assessments of age and date
reporting in DHS surveys [@pullum2006]:

- height-for-age z-scores remain more dispersed than expected, which may
  slightly inflate stunting estimates;
- the heaping of deaths at 12 months moves some deaths between the infant
  and child mortality intervals;
- the shortage of women recorded at age 50 relative to 49 points to age
  misreporting at the edge of eligibility for the women's interview.

The calibrated synthetic data meets a practical need. Because DHS files
cannot be shared, the analysis code in published papers usually cannot be
run by readers, students practice on toy data, and new methods are hard to
demonstrate. Synthetic files that reproduce the published national and
regional estimates let worked examples behave like the real survey without
containing information about any respondent. They suit teaching, software
testing and reproducible demonstrations. They should not be used for
substantive conclusions, because the associations between indicators are not
reproduced.

The case study shows how the tools work together. Caesarean delivery in
Bangladesh rose roughly ten-fold in less than two decades, part of a rapid
global increase [@betran2016]. As its use spread beyond the richest
households, absolute inequality widened while relative inequality fell.
Changes in maternal education and household wealth explain only a small part
of the rise which occurred within every group. That pattern points to
changes in health-system practice rather than in the characteristics of the
mothers, and is consistent with `r if (sji) "the earlier finding" else "our earlier finding"` that caesarean delivery
has spread through the private sector and become less tied to medical
indications [@rony2026]. Separating these components with proper standard
errors is straightforward once the design and indicator definitions are
right.

bdhs complements existing tools rather than replacing them. IPUMS-DHS
remains the better choice for comparisons between countries with harmonised
variables [@ipumsdhs], and rdhs and DHS.rates serve every DHS country
[@watson2019; @dhsrates]. bdhs reproduces DHS.rates exactly for the rates
both packages compute. Its contribution is depth for one country: every
round, the original files, validation against the official estimates, and
Bangladesh-specific harmonisation and documentation.

The study has limitations. Validation was limited to the recode files
available to the authors, mainly the children's records for the earlier
rounds, with complete sets only for 2017-18 and 2022. No files from 1996-97
were available, and its harmonisation rules, taken from the published
codebook, remain unverified. A tolerance of half a percentage point for
national estimates does not guarantee agreement for every subgroup, although
the subgroup comparisons we made agreed closely. The synthetic data
reproduces only the calibrated values. Finally, the package does not yet
produce estimates below the division level, which are increasingly needed
for planning.

# Conclusions

Analyses of the BDHS can reproduce the official estimates almost exactly.
Doing so depends on handling the ever-married samples, questionnaire changes,
country-specific conventions and survey design correctly; getting them wrong
shifts key indicators by up to ten percentage points. Writing these
decisions down once, in validated and openly available software, makes BDHS
analyses more accurate, quicker to carry out and easier to check. We suggest
that analyses of DHS data routinely report how their national estimates
compare with the official figures.
